textbookText: Diplotene of Meiosis I is characterized by following key events: a. Homologous chromosomes separate except in the region of chiasmata. b. The nuclear membrane remains intact, while the nucleolus may either be small or start to degenerate.

Fig. 1.3.3 Diplotene viii. Diakinesis (G., 'dia' = across, 'kinesis' = movement): In diakinesis stage, the final substage of prophase I in meiosis, the four parts of the tetrads are actually visible. This stage is characterized by following key events: a. Chromatids of a chromosome remain attached in the region of centromere. b. The chromosomes bivalents move towards the periphery of the nucleus. c. Chiasma shifts to the end of the chromosome. The process is known as terminalization. d. Simultaneously the nuclear membrane and nucleoli disappear. e. Spindle fibers start to develop.

Fig. 1.3.3 Diakinesis Metaphase-I During the metaphase I stage of meiosis, the nuclear membrane and nucleolus dissaper and the spindle fibers form. Homologous pairs or bivalents organize into two parallel equatorial or metaphase plates, with chromosomes or bivalents connected to the spindle fibers through their centromeres. The centromeres of bivalents are equally spaced from the equator and point toward the poles, while interzonal fibers form between the centromeres of bivalents.

a. Nuclear envelop degenerate and spindle fibres appear. b. At this stage, bivalents get arranged on the equator. c. Chromosomes occur in bivalents having chiasmata. d. Chromosomes of a bivalent get attached to spindle fibre belonging to different poles.

Anaphase-I After prophase I comes anaphase I stage which is characterized by following key events: ix. The centromere does not split, this keeps the two chromatids of each chromosome connected. x. Homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles due to the contraction of spindle fiber and the repelling force between the bivalents as chiasmata break apart. xi. The homologous chromosomes moving to opposite ends are either from the father's (paternal) or mother's (maternal) side. This process is called disjunction. xii. By the end of the phase, two groups of chromosomes are formed, each containing half the number present in the mother cell.
Telophase-I During telophase I phase of meiosis following key events take place:
a. Each end of the cell receives one set of chromosomes with two chromatids, which then unwind into chromatin threads.
b. The spindle fibers disappear. c. A nuclear membrane and a nucleolus reappear at the opposite poles, resulting in two

daughter haploid nuclei. Cytokinesis - I All cells do not go through this stage. But when they do, animal cells form a “cell furrow” and plant cells form a “cell plate”. Each new cell, called a daughter cell, gets half the number of chromosomes as the original cell, known as the mother cell.

Interphase or Interkinesis During interkinesis, the period between the first and second stages of meiosis, the cell focuses on protein and RNA production without synthesizing new DNA, known as the S-phase. This phase may vary in duration or may not occur at all. The cell prepares for the subsequent meiosis II division, ensuring the genetic material is ready for further division and the eventual production of four haploid cells from the two haploid cells produced in meiosis I. Meiosis-II This is also known as equational cell division because the number of chromosomes stays the same after the first stage of meiosis. It has two parts:

(A) Karyokinesis-II (B) Cytokinesis-II. A. Karyokinesis-II: This is divided into four phases. 1. Prophase-II: During prophase II of meiosis, the chromatids become shorter, thicker, and more visible, with each chromosome having two chromatids attached at the centromere. Additionally, the nuclear membrane and nucleolus disappear, while spindle fibers appear. The chromatids are arranged at right angles to the spindle fibers from the first stage of meiosis. 2. Metaphase-II: During metaphase II of meiosis, the nuclear membrane and nucleolus dissapera, and chromosomes align along the middle of the cell. Each chromosome's centromere splits into Biology, Grade 11 | 77
two, with each becoming the centromere for a chromatid. Additionally, each chromosome's centromere attaches to spindle fibers from both ends of the cell.

3. Anaphase-II: During anaphase II of meiosis, the separation of the centromeres of sister chromatids takes place. This leads to the division of each chromosome's centromere by the contraction of the spindle fibers and the stretching of other fibers, sister chromatids move to opposite ends of the cell. This movement is facilitated by the spindle fibers, and the separated chromatids are now referred to as chromosomes
